historical_record.description: Congregation Ohabai Shalom, formed in 1862, built its temple here in 1895 to a design by the architect Moses J. Lyon, in an eclectic style drawing on Moorish and Eastern European precedent. It is one of only three 19th-century synagogues left standing in California.

Bought in 1934 by the Soto Zen congregation as the synagogue's membership dwindled. The building housed the Japanese Zen community for more than forty years, and Shunryu Suzuki taught zazen here to students from outside the community in the 1960s and 1970s; the congregation withdrew in the 1970s to build new quarters nearby.
Sokoji Temple in Japantown, where poets and others were introduced to Zen Buddhism in the 1950s and 1960s; the San Francisco Zen Center grew out of that meeting.
Photographed, showing the Zen Soto Mission.

Offered for sale by the Redevelopment Agency in July 1975 as the Soto Zen Mission, at a minimum bid of $39,600, with priority given to holders of Residential Certificates of Preference — property owners who had lost buildings to eminent domain.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 81, Ohabai Shalome (Bush Street Temple).
The City Planning Commission approved, 3-2, the designation of the Bush Street Temple as a city landmark (Resolution 7431), after a motion to disapprove failed 2-3.
The Redevelopment Agency had bought the former Congregation Ohabai Shalome temple for retention in Western Addition Project Area A-2 and had recently sold it to the Zen Center.
The Asian American Theater Company had its offices in the former temple here and hoped to buy the building from the Redevelopment Agency for $150,000 and turn it into a theatre.

The Redevelopment Agency voted unanimously to let the Judah L. Magnes Museum's Western Jewish History Center draw up plans to buy and restore the 92-year-old former Ohabai Shalome synagogue here, on condition that its plans include space for an Asian American theatre; the Asian American Theater Company had lost its bid for the building.

The Redevelopment Agency heard three proposals to buy and restore the Bush Street Temple: a 300-seat theater from the Asian American Theater Company, an archival library of the decorative arts from Anthony Duquette and Hutton Wilkinson's Duquette Foundation for Living Arts, and a center for Jewish history from the Judah L. Magnes Museum's Western Jewish History Center.

The Redevelopment Agency agreed to sell the landmark temple, with the lot next door at 1899 Bush Street, to the Bush Street Synagogue Cultural Center, which planned to rehabilitate it and build alongside it a Jewish cultural center.
The Redevelopment Agency's 1990 agreement with the Bush Street Synagogue Cultural Center to restore the temple was terminated on February 14, 1994, for failure to perform.

The Redevelopment Agency conditionally approved the basic concept design for the Japanese American Religious Federation Assisted Living Facility on the temple's parcels at the southeast corner of Bush and Laguna Streets.

The Redevelopment Agency committed up to $2,905,555 to the Japanese American Religious Federation Assisted Living Facility to rehabilitate the temple and build beside it, 54 residential units in all on the two parcels.

The Redevelopment Agency leased the building to the Japanese American Religious Federation Assisted Living Facility for 69 years, with a 30-year option, to run 54 assisted-living units, 37 of them permanently affordable.

unknowns: The city's Japantown context statement gives 1881 Bush Street for the temple Congregation Ohabai Shalom built in 1895 and 1831 Bush Street for the same congregation's synagogue on the evidence of the 1893 and 1899 Sanborn maps. It does not reconcile the two numbers.
